I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the peculiar way we experience time, and how memory turns life into something stranger than we expect.

---

**The Compression of Years**

I turned thirty not long ago, and what struck me wasn't the number itself but the realization that my twenties had become a single, compressed feeling in my chest—not a sequence of events but a texture, like the particular weight of a blanket you haven't unfolded in years. I can tell you stories from that decade: the apartment with the broken heater in Brooklyn, the job I quit without a backup plan, the person I loved who moved to Lisbon and never quite returned, even in correspondence. But what I *experience* when I think of my twenties isn't any of these specifics. It's a mood, a color, a weather pattern. It feels like walking home at 2 AM through snow that hadn't been predicted, the city suddenly quiet and forgiving, my breath visible and my steps uncertain about whether I was going toward something or away.

This is how memory works, I think—not as a filing system but as a distillation process, slowly reducing ten thousand moments into a few drops of essential oil. The strange part is how little control we have over what gets preserved. I remember the snow walk vividly, though nothing happened. I barely remember my college graduation, which was supposed to be important. I remember the face of a stranger on a train in 2017 who was reading a book I'd never heard of, her concentration so complete that I felt I'd witnessed something private. I don't remember the name of the book. I don't remember what I read that year, though I must have read dozens of books.

The compression happens without our permission. A year of daily routines—commutes, emails, meals, sleep—reduces to almost nothing in recollection. A single week of disruption, of travel or crisis or new love, expands to fill the same space. This is why time seems to accelerate as we age: we settle into patterns, and patterned time leaves almost no trace. The years become thin. I sometimes think the whole project of adulthood, with its striving for stability, is secretly a kind of erasure, a slow fading of ourselves from our own lives.

But there's something else happening too, something I've only recently started to notice. The past doesn't just compress; it also *transforms*. Events change their emotional color over time. Humiliations become funny. Losses become soft with distance, almost beautiful in their sadness. Triumphs often shrink, revealed as smaller than they felt, or else they grow embarrassing in their ambition. I was proud of a promotion I got at twenty-six; now I mostly remember how I called my mother and couldn't tell if she understood why I was happy. The promotion is gone. The phone call remains.

This fluidity of the past means we're never quite done with it. We revisit, revise, re-feel. A friend told me recently that she'd started dreaming about her childhood home again after twenty years of absence in her sleeping life. The house in the dreams was wrong—rooms where they shouldn't be, stairs leading nowhere—but the feeling was right, the particular quality of afternoon light through curtains she'd forgotten existed. She woke up with a kind of grief for architecture, for the way spaces hold experiences we can't fully recover.

I think about this in relation to technology, which promises to preserve everything. We have photos now, videos, searchable archives of our correspondence. The paradox is that this preservation seems to make things *less* memorable, not more. When everything is saved, nothing is selected. The mind, lazy, delegates to the cloud. I have ten thousand photos on my phone and I rarely look at them. When I do, they feel like evidence of someone else's life, someone who documented more carefully than I remember living. The few photos I took with film cameras in my early twenties—expensive, limited, chosen with care—are burned into me. I don't need to look at them. I carry them.

There's a concept in physics called the arrow of time, the idea that entropy makes the past and future fundamentally different. We can remember one but only predict the other. But human time has its own arrow, and it doesn't always point the same direction. Sometimes the future feels more fixed than the past—an appointment next week, immovable, while last year remains open to interpretation. Sometimes the past feels more alive than the present, more real, more urgent. We say "move on" as if the past were a place we could leave, but we're made of it. Every cell in my body has been replaced since I was twenty, but something continues. The pattern, the distillation, the essential oil.

I find myself wanting to resist the compression, to live in ways that will leave thicker traces. But I also suspect this is a fool's errand. The most memorable times in my life were not the ones I tried to make memorable. They were the ones where I was most distracted from myself, most absorbed in something outside my own narrative. The snow walk wasn't memorable because I decided to notice it. It was memorable because, for reasons I don't understand, I was fully there—cold, uncertain, walking without a plan, the city strange and beautiful around me.

Maybe that's the only real advice, though I hesitate to give advice: be present, not for the memory but for the present itself. The memory will do what it wants. The present is the only thing we actually have, and we have it so briefly, always already becoming past, always already being distilled. I think of those medieval monks who made illuminated manuscripts, working by candlelight to preserve texts they believed sacred. They must have known that most of what they copied would be forgotten, that their careful letters would outlast their names, that the future would read what they saved without knowing who saved it. They worked anyway, in the present tense of their candlelit hours, making something beautiful for reasons they couldn't fully articulate.

I want to live like that, I think. Not for the archive, but for the hour itself. The snow is falling somewhere, always, even in summer, even in cities that have never seen snow. The walk continues. We are walking it without knowing where, without knowing whether we're going toward or away, our breath visible in the cold, our steps uncertain, the city around us suddenly quiet and strange and completely, irreplaceably itself.
